body:
OBJECTIVES
- Students explain how the Fourteenth Amendment, Plessy v. Ferguson and Executive Order 9981 framed the struggle against segregation (D2.His.1.9-12, D2.Civ.4.9-12).
- Students analyze how the Brown decision, the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and President Johnson's 1965 address changed the law, and the relationship between protest and federal action (D2.Civ.14.9-12, D2.His.14.9-12, RH.9-10.9).
- Students research a grassroots campaign and assess how the significance of its participants' actions has changed over time (D2.His.3.9-12, WHST.9-10.7, WHST.9-10.8).
- Students argue which event was the movement's most important turning point, integrating multiple sources (D2.His.16.9-12, D4.1.9-12).

MATERIALS
- Readings in the activities: The Constitution and "Separate but Equal" (Fourteenth Amendment, Harlan's dissent, Executive Order 9981), Brown v. Board, Civil Rights Act Title II, Johnson's March 15, 1965 address
- Research access: school library databases and public-domain government sources (National Archives, Library of Congress)
- A note on language: Johnson's 1965 address uses the word "Negro," the standard respectful term of the time, now outdated. Discuss historical language before reading. Note also that King's speeches and the Letter from Birmingham Jail are under copyright and are not reproduced here; your school's licensed anthologies may hold them, and they pair well with this unit.

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Equal Protection. Lesson activity: Separate but Equal. Discuss Harlan's dissent: what did it mean to be the lone dissenter in 1896?
Day 2: Law and the Movement: read Brown, Title II and Johnson's address. Build a timeline with the class from 1948 to 1965 that puts court decisions, protests and laws on separate rows.
Day 3: Finish Law and the Movement. Launch A Movement of Many: students choose a campaign (Montgomery bus boycott, Greensboro sit-ins, Freedom Rides, Birmingham campaign, Freedom Summer, Selma to Montgomery, Mendez v. Westminster, the Delano grape strike) and find sources in the library.
Day 4: Research workday and source-evaluation mini-lesson: how do you know a website is authoritative? Students draft. Research reports are due in a week.
Day 5: Unit assessment: The Movement's Turning Point (no AI help).

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: provide a curated source list for each campaign (three authoritative sources) and a note-catcher with columns for Who, What, Where, When, Why, Result.
- Support: read Johnson's address aloud; students mark each place he connects Selma to earlier American history.
- Extension: read the full Brown opinion (about eleven pages) and explain how the Court used social science evidence; compare with Harlan's dissent in Plessy.
- Extension: research how the Voting Rights Act changed Black voter registration in Mississippi between 1964 and 1968, using government data.
- Multilingual learners (ELL): pre-teach legal vocabulary with a visual (a lunch counter, a bus, a ballot). Allow research in home-language sources alongside English ones, and provide frames for the report: "The goal of the ___ was ___. Participants ___. As a result, ___."

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
Our class is studying the civil rights movement, from the desegregation of the armed forces in 1948 to the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Each student will research one campaign, such as the Montgomery bus boycott or the Greensboro sit-ins. If anyone in your family remembers these years, or other struggles for equal rights, your student would learn a great deal from hearing about them. Thank you.
title: Teacher guide: The Civil Rights Movement
